lines.text: Beyond basic colour names, English offers a sophisticated vocabulary for describing shades and tones — subtle variations that add precision and beauty to descriptions. A shade is created by adding black to a colour, making it darker: navy is a dark shade of blue, maroon is a dark shade of red, and forest green is a deep shade of green. A tint is the opposite — adding white to create a lighter version: baby blue, blush pink, and lavender are tints of their base colours. A tone is made by adding grey, creating a more muted, sophisticated version. Hue refers to the pure colour itself — the basic identity on the colour wheel. Saturation describes intensity: a highly saturated colour is vivid and bold, while a desaturated colour appears washed out or faded. English uses creative descriptors drawn from nature, food, and materials: sky blue, ocean blue, midnight blue, powder blue, and cobalt blue are all distinct shades. Reds include scarlet, crimson, burgundy, cherry, ruby, and coral. Greens range from lime and mint to emerald, olive, and khaki. Browns span chocolate, chestnut, tan, caramel, and mahogany. Greys include charcoal, slate, silver, ash, and dove grey. These nuanced colour terms are essential in fashion, interior design, art, cosmetics, and any field where precise visual communication matters.

lines.text: English borrows colour names from nature: sky blue, forest green, ocean blue, sunset orange, midnight blue, snow white, coal black, ivory, coral, salmon, lilac, lavender, plum. These natural references make descriptions vivid and universally understood.

lines.text: Gemstone colours are common in English: ruby (red), emerald (green), sapphire (blue), amethyst (purple), topaz (golden yellow), turquoise (blue-green), pearl (white), opal (iridescent). These convey luxury and precision.

lines.text: Fashion uses specific colour terms: 'ecru' (off-white), 'mauve' (muted purple), 'taupe' (grey-brown), 'teal' (blue-green), 'fuchsia' (bright pink), 'magenta' (pinkish-red). These appear in clothing catalogues and fashion magazines.

lines.text: Pantone is a global colour matching system used in design and industry. 'Pantone Colour of the Year' is announced annually and influences fashion, design, and marketing. Understanding this system is valuable in creative industries.

lines.text: English connects colours to emotions: 'feeling blue' (sad), 'seeing red' (angry), 'green with envy' (jealous), 'in the pink' (healthy), 'white with fear' (terrified), 'tickled pink' (delighted). These idioms are essential for fluent expression.
